title: Learning Paths

sections.body: Three ordered routes through the site, for readers who would rather be guided than search. Each step points to pages that already exist here, glossary entries first, so no step assumes a word you have not met. Take them in order the first time; after that, each step stands on its own.

For owners, executives and board members deciding what to adopt and what to ask. No technical background assumed.

  1. The words first. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, large language model, foundation model, hallucination, agentic AI

    Six glossary entries, each opening with a plain definition. Enough to follow every conversation that comes after, and to notice when a vendor is using a word loosely.

  2. What AI is being used for in your industry. Industry Use Cases

    Documented uses by industry, each point tied to a cited source with our summary of it. Read your own industry and one adjacent one; the adjacent one is usually where the next idea comes from.

  3. What it does to professional work. Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

    How AI is changing the work of lawyers, accountants, physicians, researchers and economists. Useful even outside those fields, because it shows where judgment stays human and where it does not.

  4. Adoption that is real, not performative. The Art of AI

    Leadership, culture and incentives decide whether AI changes how an organisation works or only how it describes itself. Read this before approving a program, so the questions you ask measure use rather than announcements.

  5. The risks you own. AI Security and Risk, prompt injection, data poisoning

    The six security domains and the failure modes a board should ask about. The glossary entries explain the two attacks every AI deployment faces.

  6. The rules that apply to you. State AI laws, EU, US and China Compared

    Which laws reach your business depends on where you operate and whom you serve. Start with your state, then the comparison if you sell abroad.

  7. What is going wrong elsewhere. AI lawsuits, AI Insurance

    Live cases and how insurers are pricing AI risk. The cheapest lessons are other people's.

For developers, analysts and technical staff building systems on models. Assumes comfort with software, not with machine learning.

  1. How the models work. Transformer, token, context window, embedding, inference, fine-tuning

    The mechanics under every system you will build. Each entry has a plain definition, then detail, then related terms to follow.

  2. Choosing a model. Large Language Models, Reasoning Models, Model Serving Providers

    What is available, who serves it, and what it costs. Pick on the task, not the headline.

  3. Judging a model on evidence. Benchmarks, benchmark, LLM as a judge

    What each benchmark measures, who ran it, and why scores from different evaluators cannot be compared. Then how to evaluate on your own data.

  4. Prompting well. Prompt Engineering

    Techniques with when they work and when they fail, and prompts by domain. Cheaper than any model upgrade.

  5. Grounding answers in your data. Retrieval augmented generation, AI and SQL

    Retrieval, vector search and letting a model query a database safely. Most business systems are this, not a new model.

  6. Agents and tools. AI agent, Model Context Protocol, AI Agents and the MCP Ecosystem

    How models call tools, and the directory of more than two thousand MCP servers with what each one can reach.

  7. Building it safely. Prompt injection, guardrails, red teaming, AI Security and Risk

    The attacks that matter for anything with tools or data access, and how to test for them before users do.

  8. Going deeper. AI Courses, AI Certifications, Research

    Courses and certifications with who issues them, and the research library when you need the primary source.

For compliance officers, risk managers, auditors and counsel responsible for how AI is controlled.

  1. The vocabulary of governance. AI governance, responsible AI, algorithmic bias, model card, red teaming

    The terms every framework and regulator uses, defined plainly.

  2. The frameworks. NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001

    The voluntary US framework most programs are organised around, and the certifiable management system standard.

  3. What assurance proves. AI Assurance Standards

    What a certificate, an impact assessment, a test report and a benchmark each show, and what they do not. Read this before relying on a vendor's claim.

  4. The law, jurisdiction by jurisdiction. EU AI Act, EU, US and China Compared, State AI laws

    The EU Act with its current dates, the three regimes side by side, then the states. Colorado and Texas are the ones most programs now build to.

  5. Everything in force, in one table. AI Policy Ledger

    Every law, rule and executive action the site tracks, with who it applies to, when it takes effect and its penalty ceiling as the text states it.

  6. How it is enforced. AI Enforcement Actions, Agency enforcement, AI lawsuits

    FTC and SEC actions that name AI, the other agencies, and the private litigation. Enforcement shows which duties are real.

  7. What is changing now. Colorado ADMT rulemaking, AI news

    Open rulemakings with their deadlines, and the daily briefing for what moved this week.

sections.h: How these paths are kept current
sections.body: The paths are chosen and ordered by the editor. Every page they point to is rebuilt from its sources on its own schedule, shown on the Data Quality page, so a path stays current as the pages under it change. If a step points somewhere that no longer serves its purpose, please tell us at theworldofai@inkboxmail.com.

description: Three guided routes through The World of AI: for business leaders, for people building with AI, and for governance and compliance, each an ordered set of steps through pages on this site.
